en: Bhāṣikasūtra 1.1: Now follows the rule for the phonetic refinement of Brāhmaṇa accents.
1.3 The accentuation of mantras has been explained.
1.4 By that [rule], it is established here [for brāhmaṇas].
1.5 The acute (udātta) and grave (anudātta) accents belong to the spoken language (bhāṣika), as does their combination (saṃdhi).

1.6 An udātta [vowel] occurs between two anudātta vowels. 1.7 It does not occur when preceded by ā or pra and followed by a verb (ākhyāta). 1.8 Nor does it occur in a compound, even when not followed by a verb.
1.9 And there is no such thing as an unprecedented compound. 1.10 [The elision of] *jāti*, *abhinihita*, *kṣaipra*, and *praśliṣṭa* [svaritas]. 1.11 For *uta*, *yaḥ*, *maḥ*, *naḥ*, and *saḥ*.
1.12 For some [teachers], there is the vowel *oṃ*. 1.13 This is acute (*udātta*).
1.14 And it is also circumflex (*svarita*) and grave (*anudātta*).

1.15 A vowel that is not final [in a word] is either udātta or anudātta. 1.16 In the case of conjunct consonants, the final vowel is [anudātta]. 1.17 And in the colloquial (bhāṣika) style, both [the initial and final vowels of a word] are [anudātta].
1.18 Even of a single [syllable];
1.19 And of a svarita that is abhinihita;
1.20 And of those [svaritas] preceding the last one, as well as those immediately following them, there is a tremor (kampana).
1.21 [The substitution of *svarita* occurs] for an *anudātta* that is preceded by an *udātta*.
1.22 [The substitution of *svarita* occurs] also for a *svarita* that is preceded by an *udātta*.
1.23 Regarding this, there are differing opinions concerning whether the final *udātta* becomes *anudātta* in each case.
2.1 Now, the verbal roots (vikaraṇas) of the verb forms;
2.2 beginning with the meaning;
2.3 beginning with the foot.
2.4 for indeed;
2.5 come now;
2.7 *kuvit* 2.8 *aha* 2.9 in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*)
2.10 With the sound of an address; 2.11 That which is desired to be known; 2.12 That which is deliberated upon.
2.13 Determination;
2.14 Connection; 2.15 Application.
2.16 The remainder of the sentence; 2.17 The suffix; 2.18 These [syllables] undergo modification up to sixteen syllables.
2.19 Bhāradvāja says [the suffix *ka* is applied] up to twenty-five years of age. 2.20 Aupāśibi says [it is applied] up to thirty-two years of age.
2.21 In the case of compounds ending in *maryādā*, *asthi*, and *pad*, as well as in the case of many [words], the first member undergoes modification.
2.22 "All [the suffixes]"—this is the view of Aupaśivi.
3.1 But in the case of application (*viniyoga*), the preceding word [is significant].
3.2 And also in the case of two things that are desired to be known.
3.3 And in the case of two [words] that are not separated;
3.4 and in the case of those that have been deliberated upon and combined;

3.5 Regarding etymological definition (*nirvacana*), Bhāradvāja maintains that a suffix (*anubandha*), a remainder of a sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), a limitative particle (*avadhi*), and a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) do not undergo modification.

3.6 Those who speak more, those who speak better, and those who speak less are not to be determined [as superior]. 3.7 For one of the [three] initial [types of speakers], whichever is intended for completion does not undergo modification.
3.8 Between two words, that which has fewer vowels among those beginning with a vowel remains in its original form.
3.9 Bhāradvāja maintains that when a vowel and a non-vowel, both having equal duration, meet, the former [is not desired as nasalized].
3.10 A word is of four kinds according to its meaning, and it may be reversed. 3.11 A guttural vowel [is nasalized] before a *ṛ*, *ṝ*, or a similar sound.
3.12 There is elision of the letter *va* at the end of a word when it occurs between vowels.

3.13 The remainder [of the rules] follows from the general grammatical treatises (*sāmānya-śāstra*). 3.14 The letters *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *lṛ* are the sustainers (*dhāraṇā*) of the vowel class (*avarṇa*).
3.15 For the Śatapatha, Tāṇḍya, and Bhāllavi [Brāhmaṇas], the accent is that of the Brāhmaṇa.
3.16 There are seven [notes] for the Sāmans.
3.17 [These are] Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, Pañcama, Dhaivata, and Niṣāda.
3.18 Their sources:
3.19 The *ṣaḍja* [note] arises from the throat; 3.20 the *ṛṣabha* [note] arises from the head.
3.21 Gāndhāra arises from the nose; 3.22 Madhyama arises from the chest;
3.23 Pañcama arises from the chest, the head, and the throat.
3.24 Dhaivata [arises] from the forehead;
3.25 Niṣāda [arises] from everywhere;
3.26 The tone of the Brāhmaṇas is like the tone of the mantras for the Carakas.
3.27 Among those [Vedic schools], for the Khāṇḍikheyas and the Aukheyas, there is also the fourfold accentuation (*cātuḥsvarya*) in some instances.
3.28 For others, it is monotone (*tāna*), which is the accent of the Brāhmaṇas. 3.29 It is monotone for the Aṅgas and Upāṅgas; it is monotone for the Aṅgas and Upāṅgas—so it is said.
Thus ends the Bhāṣika-Parisiṣṭa-sūtra composed by the venerable great sage Kātyāyana.
